name: Topical melatonin hair

lead: Topical melatonin is a solution applied to the scalp by some people with androgenetic alopecia, hoping to slow thinning and keep a fuller head of hair. Melatonin is the body's sleep-timing hormone and also an antioxidant in lab tests.
The off-label idea draws on those antioxidant properties. Melatonin has been examined in small studies as a scalp solution, and this entry draws on general reference information only.

paras: People apply it as a scalp solution in a regular routine, sometimes alongside other hair-loss treatments. Users generally expect results, if any, to take months.
Melatonin is sold over the counter as a supplement in many countries. Scalp-specific safety data were not reviewed.

angle.text: Some people with androgenetic alopecia apply melatonin to the scalp hoping to slow thinning and keep a fuller head of hair. It is an off-label idea drawn from melatonin's antioxidant properties acting on the follicle. Small studies have looked at it for this use.

lead: Topical melatonin for hair refers to melatonin solutions applied to the scalp by people with androgenetic alopecia who hope to slow thinning and thicken hair, usually alongside established treatments. Melatonin is a hormone made mainly by the pineal gland that regulates sleep-wake timing, and it is also an in vitro antioxidant.[1]

Interest in the scalp comes from the idea that hair follicles are themselves sites of melatonin activity and that its antioxidant properties could protect them; proponents point to this reasoning, while reviews describe the hair evidence as varying in strength.[1][2] Wikipedia's article on pattern hair loss lists topical melatonin among androgen-independent treatments, alongside the established options of minoxidil, finasteride, dutasteride, hair transplantation and low-level laser therapy.[3]

A 2026 systematic review with network meta-analysis of off-label androgenetic alopecia therapies reported that topical melatonin was among those that appeared effective for male pattern loss on 6-month change in hair density, with topical 5% minoxidil ranked most effective and the authors calling for higher-quality comparative trials.[2] A 2026 case series has also described topical melatonin in people with hair graying.[2]
infobox: Among off-label topicals that appeared effective at 6 months (2026)[2]

paras: Pattern hair loss is the most common cause of hair loss; by age 50 about half of men and a quarter of women are affected, according to Wikipedia.[3] It results from genetic sensitivity to androgens, mainly dihydrotestosterone formed by 5-alpha-reductase in the scalp, which shrinks follicles over time (miniaturisation); the article also mentions possible roles for oxidative stress, the scalp microbiome and Wnt signalling as less established factors.[3] The oxidative stress idea is the reasoning proponents give for trying an antioxidant like melatonin on the scalp.

Melatonin acts as an agonist at MT1 and MT2 receptors and, in vitro, scavenges free radicals and promotes antioxidant enzyme expression.[1] Proponents of scalp use point to these antioxidant properties; whether they translate to hair growth is a question for clinical trials.

A 2026 systematic review with network meta-analyses covering 23 studies, 15 of them off-label therapies, reported that topical melatonin appeared effective for male androgenetic alopecia based on mean 6-month change in total hair density; topical minoxidil 5% ranked highest, and the authors called for higher-quality comparative trials.[2] A 2026 clinical dermatology review names androgenetic alopecia as an area of interest for topical melatonin and says the strength of evidence varies across indications.[2] A 2026 case series examined topical melatonin for hair graying repigmentation.[2] Other 2025 to 2026 network meta-analyses of conventional and non-conventional over-the-counter treatments for male androgenetic alopecia, and reviews of melatonin in dermatology and of the cutaneous melatoninergic system, appear in the literature listing.[2]

Topical melatonin is mentioned in hair-loss communities as an inexpensive add-on to established treatments such as minoxidil. Evidence cited in these discussions tends to be the general pharmacology of melatonin and the small published datasets above.[1][2]

Melatonin is sold over the counter as an oral supplement in many countries, and scalp solutions are marketed by cosmetic and compounding suppliers; no regulator-approved hair-loss indication for topical melatonin was identified.[1] Researchers who published a 2026 review of cutaneous melatonin biology place it within a wider interest in using topical melatonin for photoprotection and skin rejuvenation as well as hair.[2][2]

claims.claim: Melatonin on the scalp helps hair growth as an add-on to other treatments

timeline.event: Melatonin first isolated by the team of Aaron B. Lerner.[1]
Network meta-analysis lists topical melatonin among off-label topicals that appeared effective at 6 months, below minoxidil.[2]
